## Data:

Information on all the variables:

| Variable | Predictor or Response | Data Type | Discrete or Continuous | Values/Units |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| Fatal Avalanche Incidents | Response | integer | discrete | \[0, 1, 2, ...\] |
| EL Nino Phase | Predictor | categorical | discrete | \["nino", "int", "nina"\] |
| Average Snowfall | Predictor | double | continuous | xx.xx inches |
| State | Predictor | Informational | discrete | \["CA", "CO", "NM"\] |
| Visit Frequency | Predictor | categorical | discrete | \["high", "low"\] |

- **Fatal Avalanche Incidents:** This is our response variable. It is a count of how many incidents occurred in that year. Because it is a count, it is only integers, and it approximates a Poisson distribution.
- **ENSO Phase:** This is our primary predictor, and it is categorical. For our intents and purposes, we classify each year as either "La Nina", "Intermittent", or "El Nino" based on the Niño 3.4 Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly (SSTA) data. We determine the phase by taking the yearly average SSTA and classifying it based on that. This variable was chosen because it is our main predictor.
- **Average Snowfall:** This is our only continuous predictor. It is a yearly average of snowfall for the state that we calculate based on snowfall averages at one weather station per state. Snowfall ebbs and flows just as much as the ENSO phase does. This is an important variable to include because there have been La Niña years that have had lots of snowfall. In our model, this will allow us to get a more accurate reading on the relationship between the ENSO Phase variable and our response. It can be considered a **mediator** variable.
- **State:** This is an informational variable. The state is merely a proxy variable for the visit frequency. We only look at three states: California, Colorado, and New Mexico. These three states were chosen because they fall along the storm track of an El Niño phase, so they tend to receive the same storms.
- **Visit Frequency:** This is another categorical predictor. The three states are each classified as either high or low visitor frequency. This variable was chosen because a region with more visitors is bound to have more avalanche incidents simply due to chance. In order to remove this noise, visit frequency was included as a variable.

## Statistical Model Choice:

Generalized linear model using a Poisson distribution: our response variable is the fatal accident count, so it is an integer from 0 +n as n -\> inf

## Analysis
For this analysis, it's very important that all this data is combined into one dataset. For ease of plotting and performing the generalized linear model, it is important the data is consolidated. The following is an example diagram showing how each row of the final DataFrame should look:

| year | fatality_count | enso_phase | snow_in | state | visitors |
|------|----------------|------------|---------|-------|----------|
| 2023 | 14             | nino       | 715     | CA    | high     |
| ...  | ...            | ...        | ...     | ...   | ...      |

Heres how we did that:

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| output: false

# Yearly sum of avalanche incidents per state
year_av <- avalanche_data |> summarize(fatality_count = sum(Killed), .by = c(AvyYear, State))

# Yearly mean of ENSO data with classification of nino, nina. or int
year_enso <- nino_data |>  
    summarize(avg_sst_anm = mean(sst_anomaly), .by = year) |>
    mutate(phase = case_when(
        avg_sst_anm >= 0.5 ~ "nino",
        avg_sst_anm <= -0.5 ~ "nina",
        .default = "int"
    ))

# Yearly sum of snowfall at each location
ca_snow$state <- "CA"
co_snow$state <- "CO"
nm_snow$state <- "NM"

year_snow <- ca_snow |>
    bind_rows(co_snow) |> 
    bind_rows(nm_snow) |> 
    select(state, year, snow_inches) |> 
    summarize(total_snow = sum(snow_inches), .by = c(year, state))
```
